2 · Each flagged moment: from curve to note

drop0:13
1 · what the curve showedThe opening frame loses 68,188 viewers in one second as the cold open ends and the premise restatement begins (*11.04% stop rate, 90.0% remaining*). 2 · evidence at that second“that's just the start” (transcript) 3 · why (the check or the quote)The hook lists the mods then pivots to 'and well, that's just the start of a long list of changes', signaling setup rather than payoff. 4 · how (the next move)Hold this one — 0:15 retention sits at 90.0% versus the 95.1% channel median, but the loss rate itself is only 1.1x channel norm and typical for the channel. 5 · rationaleThis is the channel's standing opening habit, not a defect unique to this video, and the surrounding numbers do not justify surgery.
drop3:37
1 · what the curve showedThe video sheds almost a fifth of its remaining audience in 27 seconds as it pivots from the failed power-on to a sponsor read (*8.65% stop rate, 11.6x the channel norm, 138,537 viewers*). 2 · evidence at that second“this did not go according to plan” (transcript) 3 · why (the check or the quote)The cliffhanger 'this did not go according to plan' is immediately swapped for a Boot.dev pitch that opens 'debugging physical hardware can be an absolute pain'. 4 · how (the next move)Test moving the Boot.dev read to just before the HDMI reveal at 4:39, keeping the failure teased and unresolved across the read. 5 · rationaleAds hold best at peak anticipation; here the read fires right after the tease, releasing suspense before viewers get any payoff. cautionConfirm Boot.dev has no contractual placement window; if it must stay pre-4:00, shorten the segue rather than move the read.
peak4:58
1 · what the curve showedAudience climbs 11.6% and holds for 31 samples right after the HDMI fix reveal (*39,516 viewers regained, 51.0% present, sustained ~30 seconds*). 2 · evidence at that second“it boots just fine” (transcript) 3 · why (the check or the quote)Viewers rewind to the payoff line 'HDMI 2 here... it boots just fine' that resolves the cliffhanger the sponsor read interrupted. 4 · how (the next move)Front-load this reveal structure in future builds: tease the failure, run the read, then deliver the fix in one clean on-screen beat. 5 · rationaleA sustained 31-sample lift on a resolution shot is the specific signature of a rewatched payoff, and it names what the audience came for.
peak15:48
1 · what the curve showedA small lift of 2.9% appears on the wire-fit close-up before the case-design section (*9,693 viewers regained, 45.7% present, held one sample*). 2 · evidence at that second“how perfectly our wires fit” (transcript) 3 · why (the check or the quote)The line 'look at how perfectly our wires fit now' lands on a visible before/after, a moment viewers scrub back to inspect. 4 · how (the next move)Show the wire-fit close-up a beat longer and cut the following design monologue in tight over the print, preserving the visual proof. 5 · rationaleThe one-sample hold means the interest is on the shot itself, not the narration that follows, so protect the shot and shorten the talk.
drop16:01
1 · what the curve showedA short 14-second window loses 21,619 viewers as the build shifts from wiring cleanup to case-design narration (*1.32% stop rate, 29.9x the surrounding baseline, 2.3x channel norm*). 2 · evidence at that second“some unique challenges” (transcript) 3 · why (the check or the quote)The narration moves from a resolved fix ('this was a pretty easy fix') into abstract design talk about switch extensions and clearance, with no visible progress beat. 4 · how (the next move)Tighten 15:54-16:15 by cutting the 'unique challenges' verbal setup and jumping straight to the 'copy Nintendo's homework' line over the print shot. 5 · rationaleThe drop lands on a stretch of describing a problem before showing the solution; collapsing to the solution removes the dead air the numbers flag. cautionConfirm the switch-extension detail is not referenced later; if it is, keep one shot of the moving parts instead of the narration.
peak20:19
1 · what the curve showedAudience rises 2.4% during the Perfect Dark overclock demo (*8,201 viewers regained, 46.3% present, held two samples*). 2 · evidence at that second“made the high rise mode playable” (transcript) 3 · why (the check or the quote)The claim 'the CPU overclock actually made the high rise mode playable' pairs a specific game and mode with a measurable result. 4 · how (the next move)Move a comparable overclock-vs-stock side-by-side into the first 60 seconds of the next build video as a proof-of-payoff teaser. 5 · rationaleReplay peaks on named, measurable results are the strongest evidence of what this audience will rewind for, and they belong earlier in the promise.

2 · Each flagged moment: from curve to note

drop0:15
1 · what the curve showedThe opening 17 seconds sheds more of the room than the channel's other intros normally do (*1.4x channel norm, 211,795 viewers, 41% vs similar*). 2 · evidence at that second“Finally, somebody is going to bring” (transcript) 3 · why (the check or the quote)The hook front-loads four promises then restates the premise the thumbnail already sold before any visual payoff lands. 4 · how (the next move)Cut 0:22-0:31 and rejoin on 'using one of these devices in 2026 is a bit of a rough experience' to open on the real problem. 5 · rationaleThe intro's job is context, stakes and goal fast — reminiscing about the original announcement delays the first payoff the thumbnail promised.
drop5:03
1 · what the curve showedThis 48-second stretch actually loses viewers slower than the channel typically does here (*0.5x channel norm, 8,521 viewers, 63% vs similar*). 2 · evidence at that second“secret to unlocking your Xbox” (transcript) 3 · why (the check or the quote)The LPC port setup lands cleanly — '15 contacts are the secret to unlocking your Xbox' — teasing mod chips without overstaying the exposition. 4 · how (the next move)Leave this beat as scored and use its 5-second information batching as the model for the 21:32 RGB spec read. 5 · rationaleThe numbers say this is how the channel's audience wants exposition delivered; do not re-cut a beat outperforming its own norm.
drop6:55
1 · what the curve showedA 32-second block tracks the channel's normal loss rate for this position (*3.2x surrounding stop rate, 8,469 viewers, 58% vs similar*). 2 · evidence at that second“twice before without any luck” (transcript) 3 · why (the check or the quote)The RAM history recap runs — 'Microsoft decided to simply remove half of the Ram chips' — as setup for the double-RAM mod that pays off later. 4 · how (the next move)Keep the historical beat but tighten 7:16-7:23 where the 'twice before without any luck' aside repeats the earlier 'white whale' framing. 5 · rationaleThis drop is at channel norm, so surgery is unwarranted; only trim the one line that repeats an already-established stake.
drop9:34
1 · what the curve showedA 64-second block loses viewers at 8.6x the channel's normal rate for this position (*31.2x surrounding stop rate, 93,663 viewers, 52% vs similar*). 2 · evidence at that second“But first, I actually have a big announcement” (transcript) 3 · why (the check or the quote)The RAM-mod payoff is teased ('trying to do for over two years') then interrupted by a Modders Masterclass announcement before the reveal lands. 4 · how (the next move)Move the Masterclass pitch to after the '1, 2' boot test resolves, and run it split-screen over the next soldering B-roll instead of stopping the story. 5 · rationaleAds placed right at the height of anticipation hold; cutting away the moment before a two-year payoff releases viewers exactly when tension peaked. cautionVerify the Masterclass slot is self-owned rather than a contracted sponsor read; if contracted, A/B the cross-cut placement and keep it if drop-off falls below 4.90%.
drop15:57
1 · what the curve showedThis 16-second beat loses viewers slower than the channel typically does here (*0.7x channel norm, 8,356 viewers, 60% vs similar*). 2 · evidence at that second“two dying fans that are making a ton of noise” (transcript) 3 · why (the check or the quote)The fan-swap segue lands cleanly with a visible reason — 'not one, but two dying fans that are making a ton of noise' — before the adapter print. 4 · how (the next move)Leave this beat intact; use its 'problem stated, part shown, install' cadence to rebuild the 19:56 heat-shrink tangent. 5 · rationaleThis is the channel's habitual transition pattern working; the numbers do not license a cut here.
drop19:56
1 · what the curve showedA 16-second beat loses viewers at 1.7x the channel's norm for this position (*6.3x surrounding stop rate, 16,843 viewers, 59% vs similar*). 2 · evidence at that second“one of my favorite new time savers” (transcript) 3 · why (the check or the quote)The heat-shrink connector explainer is a tool tangent — 'ring of low temperature solder', 'airtight seal' — with no visible Xbox progression on screen. 4 · how (the next move)Cut 19:47-20:15 down to a five-second insert of the finished splice and rejoin on 'my doorbell rang' to preserve the package reveal. 5 · rationaleSomething new should visibly change every ~5 seconds; a 30-second product spec on a generic connector is repetition, not progression.
drop21:32
1 · what the curve showedA 16-second block loses viewers at 1.3x the channel's norm for the position (*7.2x surrounding stop rate, 9,431 viewers, 55% vs similar*). 2 · evidence at that second“seven for each controller port” (transcript) 3 · why (the check or the quote)The RGB kit spec sheet is read aloud — 'seven for each controller port, as well as a big ring of LEDs' — before any light is shown on. 4 · how (the next move)Cut 21:17-21:29 and jump straight from 'add some RGB' to the invasive controller-port modification, saving the LED count for a payoff insert once lit. 5 · rationaleDopamine spikes at the announcement of a reward, not the spec — front-loading the parts list burns anticipation the reveal later needs.
peak23:24
1 · what the curve showedViewers scrubbed back into this stretch and stayed (*2.2% of the audience present rejoined, 9,167 viewers regained, 63% vs similar*). 2 · evidence at that second“part of me wondered if I might not ever finish it” (transcript) 3 · why (the check or the quote)The final-assembly bonus features are being unveiled — 'drive caddy', 'customizable little nameplates' — the payoff for the two-year build arc. 4 · how (the next move)Add an on-screen '3D print files available' card at this exact beat and hold it through 23:30 to convert the rewatch into a download action. 5 · rationalePeak-end rule: the emotional high sits here, so reinforcing the tangible takeaway at the exact rewind point compounds satisfaction into the next video.
peak23:40
1 · what the curve showedViewers rewound to this stretch and held (*2.3% of the audience present rejoined, 9,615 viewers regained, 64% vs similar*). 2 · evidence at that second“so that it could be illuminated” (transcript) 3 · why (the check or the quote)The transparent-plastic case rework and illuminated jewel are being described — 'mount the stellar RGB ring kit directly below the X boxes jewel'. 4 · how (the next move)Cut a 3-second hero shot of the illuminated jewel and use it as the thumbnail-adjacent frame at 0:12 when 'over 35% smaller' is claimed. 5 · rationaleViewers rewound specifically for the finished aesthetic; showing it early converts curiosity into a specific reveal they will wait for.
drop23:56

peak23:56
1 · what the curve showedViewers scrubbed back to this beat and stayed (*2.5% of the audience present rejoined, 10,844 viewers regained, 64% vs similar*). 2 · evidence at that second“greeted with the XBMC4Gamers homepage” (transcript) 3 · why (the check or the quote)The 'X-Box Pro' boot lands and the XBMC4Gamers homepage tour begins — the moment the entire build resolves into a working, launchable console. 4 · how (the next move)Tease this exact frame — 'X-Box Pro' boot into the XBMC4Gamers homepage — in the first 15 seconds as the concrete promise the video is heading toward. 5 · rationaleA reveal that earns rewinds is an asset; front-loading a glimpse of it turns the whole video into structured anticipation for a moment viewers already want.

I can't believe I beat Microsoft to it...

published 2026-06-08 · in the recent-cohort window the advice is computed over · analysed 2026-08-26

1 · Retention breakdown

curve100 samples, stored one per percent runtime20:37 gone by 0:3030.9% at halfway38% still watching methodhazard = (present before − present after) ÷ present before at each moment; baseline = mean hazard of the previous 5 moments, floored; flagged when the excess viewers lost beyond baseline ranks high; a rise is a rewind only when no comparable drop precedes it and the lift survives the next sample

Red marks are flagged drops, green are earned rewinds. Hover a mark for its note.

2 · Each flagged moment: from curve to note

drop0:11
1 · what the curve showedThe first-second drop takes 24,015 viewers as the room settles from 100% to 92.0% (*8.7x surrounding rate, 1.0x channel norm*). 2 · evidence at that second“recreate one of the most legendary Xboxes” (transcript) 3 · why (the check or the quote)The opening lands the premise cleanly with "recreate one of the most legendary Xboxes" and this intro loses only 14.0% versus the channel's 22.5% average for intros. 4 · how (the next move)Hold the current cold open; do not recut — this intro already beats 77 of 96 sibling videos by 0:30. 5 · rationaleIntros are judged against the channel's intro cohort, and this one runs at 0.6x the channel's typical intro loss, so surgery would risk a proven opener.
drop2:28
1 · what the curve showedA 12-second dip in the setup phase loses 4,353 viewers (*2.7x surrounding rate, 1.3x channel norm, audience 49.8% to 47.7%*). 2 · evidence at that second“not as easy as you might think” (transcript) 3 · why (the check or the quote)The 3D-scanner explanation stalls on process caveats: "this process is not as easy as you might think" before any scan payoff lands. 4 · how (the next move)Cut 2:41-2:57 scanner-limitations tangent and jump from "materialize on screen" straight to the assembled 3D model appearing on screen. 5 · rationalePacing is the flow of NEW information; the caveat block adds no new visual and this drop runs above channel norm, unlike the surrounding intro cohort.
drop3:55
1 · what the curve showedA 12-second dip loses 3,181 viewers in the base-design section (*4.0x surrounding rate, 1.0x channel norm, audience 45.5% to 44.2%*). 2 · evidence at that second“disappointed with this initial test print” (transcript) 3 · why (the check or the quote)The narrator dwells on a failed test print: "I was so disappointed with this initial test print" before the fix arrives. 4 · how (the next move)Compress 4:02-4:22 wobble-fest diagnosis to a 5-second montage of the failing print plus one line, then jump to the revised design. 5 · rationaleStripping-down phases (teardown and failure analysis) lose people; compressing them preserves the positive-progression beat that holds retention.
drop4:57
1 · what the curve showedA 12-second dip loses 3,359 viewers around the quarter mark (*3.7x surrounding rate, 0.9x channel norm, audience 44.4% to 43.0%*). 2 · evidence at that second“the top of our Xbox tower” (transcript) 3 · why (the check or the quote)The build transitions from base to fan housing with a plain segue: "the next thing we need to work on is the top of our Xbox tower". 4 · how (the next move)Cut the verbal segue at 4:54-5:02 and hard-cut from the base solidifying to the fan housing already mid-print with on-screen label "fan housing v1". 5 · rationaleSomething should visibly change every ~5 seconds; a spoken transition with no new visual is a valley, and pattern-interrupting with a zoom or angle change holds retention.
drop6:48
1 · what the curve showedA 49-second stretch bleeds the largest chunk of the video (*23.3x the surrounding stop rate, 35,276 viewers, audience 41.4% to 29.5%*). 2 · evidence at that second“stripped out a tiny screw” (transcript) 3 · why (the check or the quote)The build pauses for a Fanttik sponsor read opened with the classic pain-point pitch: "Have you ever stripped out a tiny screw". 4 · how (the next move)Test cross-cutting the read over the outer-panel CNC work at 8:28-8:56, opening on "cutting clear acrylic with a laser is kind of problematic" instead of the screw pitch. 5 · rationaleA straight read costs 10-20% of remaining audience; cross-cutting with progressing story cuts that to ~2%, and this read currently sits right after the tower reveal, releasing tension. cautionConfirm Fanttik contract allows repositioning and a story-led opener; if the first line is contractually locked, negotiate a new opener before re-editing.
peak8:27
1 · what the curve showedThe audience rises 15.5% here, pulling back 15,326 viewers to 33.8% present (*63rd percentile vs similar videos*). 2 · evidence at that second“use my codes to save” (transcript) 3 · why (the check or the quote)Viewers scrub back over the Fanttik discount-code beat: "use my codes to save on any one of these awesome tools" to catch the promo they missed. 4 · how (the next move)Add a persistent on-screen chyron with the code and a timestamp chapter marker at 8:18, so returning viewers don't have to hunt. 5 · rationaleThe rewind proves demand for the code; surfacing it visually captures the intent without forcing a scrub, and reduces the surrounding stop rate.
peak8:40
1 · what the curve showedA second replay peak lifts the audience 13.0%, pulling back 14,819 viewers to 38.2% present (*68th percentile vs similar videos*). 2 · evidence at that second“cut my panels out of some larger acrylic sheets” (transcript) 3 · why (the check or the quote)Viewers rewind to catch the acrylic-panel plan: "cut my panels out of some larger acrylic sheets", the first concrete step toward the promised clear build. 4 · how (the next move)Front-load a 3-second blueprint graphic of the acrylic-panel plan at 8:38 so first-pass viewers absorb it without rewinding. 5 · rationaleA reveal that earns rewinds is an asset; announcing the plan visually satisfies the interest without depending on audio-only comprehension.
drop12:22
1 · what the curve showedA 12-second dip loses 3,617 viewers as the audience slips 38.3% to 37.1% (*13.1x surrounding rate, 1.1x channel norm*). 2 · evidence at that second“But first, while we have this” (transcript) 3 · why (the check or the quote)The narrator interrupts an imminent clear-panel reveal to pivot: "But first, while we have this thing in a half assembled state", deferring the promised payoff. 4 · how (the next move)Move the Noctua cooling upgrade earlier, before the painted-parts tease at 12:06, so the clear-panel reveal at 12:16 lands without a deferral beat. 5 · rationaleNever resolve or delay a teased payoff with runtime spent — dopamine spikes at the announcement, and stalling here sheds viewers who were queued for the reveal. cautionVerify the cooling upgrade doesn't require the half-assembled state shown at 12:23; if it does, keep sequence and shorten the deferral to one sentence.
peak15:28

Yes, okay, I think it works", the payoff to the wiring section. 4 · how (the next move)Start an anticipatory riser at 15:08 during the wiring-completion beat so the fan-spin payoff lands with buildup already in the room. 5 · rationaleRisers starting ~20 seconds before a key moment flatten retention through the buildup and hold up to ~10% more of the room to the payoff.
peak15:40

The spoken opening (first 60s, stored for the opening probes)

drop0:13
1 · what the curve showedOne in ten viewers leaves in the first frame, matching the channel's normal opening loss (*10.24% stop rate, 1.0x the channel norm, 36,707 viewers*). 2 · evidence at that second“fix the biggest problem with modern Hi-Fi” (transcript) 3 · why (the check or the quote)The opening states the premise the thumbnail already sold — "we are going to fix the biggest problem with modern Hi-Fi speakers" — before showing anything unusual. 4 · how (the next move)Trial an open on the finished panel-speaker playing music in an impossibly thin form factor, then cut to the desk-space problem as justification within 5 seconds. 5 · rationaleThis intro loses 15.1% versus a 22.5% channel average for intros, so it is already better than typical — but the channel's best intro loses 0%, and out-of-context visual hooks close the interest gap faster than restated premises. cautionConfirm the finished-panel shot does not spoil the reveal the video is structured toward; if it does, use a teardown or exciter close-up instead.
drop4:57
1 · what the curve showedThe sponsor read collapses the audience the moment it starts, losing 64,452 viewers in 28 seconds (*20.0x the surrounding stop rate, 9.3x the channel norm*). 2 · evidence at that second“And that's opera. The sponsor” (transcript) 3 · why (the check or the quote)The read opens on the sponsor name with no bridge from the build — "And that's opera. The sponsor of today's video" — exactly the cold-open pattern that costs 10-20% of the room. 4 · how (the next move)Rebuild the read as a cross-cut: keep the panel research/painting footage running under the Opera pitch, and open the read on the research problem, not the brand name. 5 · rationaleCross-cutting an ad with the progressing main story cuts sponsor loss from 10-20% to ~2%; this read is currently losing 15pp of a 48.4% audience. cautionVerify the sponsor contract allows a cross-cut open that delays the brand name by a few seconds; if not, negotiate the first sentence rather than moving it.
peak6:21
1 · what the curve showedAudience rises 30.0% and holds for 72 samples the instant the sponsor read ends and the build resumes (*42,518 viewers regained, 64th percentile vs similar videos*). 2 · evidence at that second“let's get back to talking about the exciter” (transcript) 3 · why (the check or the quote)The line "So that is it for our panels. Now let's get back to talking about the exciter" is an explicit end-of-ad signal, and viewers who scrubbed past the read return here. 4 · how (the next move)Front-load an on-screen countdown timer during the Opera read so scrubbers land on the resume line at 6:20 instead of overshooting into the exciter fix. 5 · rationaleThe rewind proves viewers value the exciter content but not the read; a visible sponsor-time countdown converts the same scrub behavior into shorter skips and higher held audience.
peak6:35
1 · what the curve showedA second rise of 12.5% lands on the exciter failure reveal and holds 67 samples (*22,943 viewers regained, 70th percentile vs similar videos*). 2 · evidence at that second“fall off panels after a very short honeymoon” (transcript) 3 · why (the check or the quote)The reveal that the included tape fails — "these exciter love to fall off panels after a very short honeymoon period" — is a rewind-worthy practical warning viewers scrub back to catch. 4 · how (the next move)Tease this failure at 0:45 with a 2-second shot of an exciter falling off, then pay it off here; structure the video so the fix earns the rewind. 5 · rationaleReveals that earn rewinds are assets — teasing early and structuring toward them extends the anticipation window and lifts retention through the middle third.
peak21:11
1 · what the curve showedAudience ticks up 3.6% for only 3 samples on the EQ automation line (*7,511 viewers regained, 62nd percentile vs similar videos*). 2 · evidence at that second“automatically create a custom EQ map” (transcript) 3 · why (the check or the quote)The moment describes automating a custom EQ map — "automatically create a custom EQ map that's tailored not just to your specific speakers, but also to the room" — a copyable technical step viewers rewind to note. 4 · how (the next move)Show the actual EQ map on screen with the software name visible for a full 5 seconds here, so the rewind pays off in one viewing instead of forcing a second. 5 · rationaleThe 3-sample hold is short because the visual moves on before the rewinder can copy it; extending the screen time of the copyable asset converts a tick into a plateau.
drop21:25
1 · what the curve showedA 30-second black gap between "replacing" and the reflection segment sheds 25,779 viewers across 71 seconds (*9.5x surrounding stop rate, but 0.9x the channel norm here*). 2 · evidence at that second“finally ready to compare these new speakers” (transcript) 3 · why (the check or the quote)The narration signals the video is ending — "finally ready to compare these new speakers to my old ones, which they will hopefully be replacing" — then goes silent for 30 seconds before the verdict. 4 · how (the next move)Cut the 21:06-21:36 silence entirely and jump straight from "replacing" into the honest verdict, so the comparison lands before viewers sense the outro. 5 · rationaleRetention drops the moment viewers sense the video is ending; a 30-second dead gap after an ending-signal sentence gives every hesitant viewer permission to leave before the payoff.

drop0:11

drop2:36

peak10:59

peak17:34

drop17:58

1 · what the curve showedFour viewers scrub back in the first minute, lifting the audience 2.8% while holding 60.4% present (*56% vs similar videos*). 2 · evidence at that secondno transcript line available; the note uses check-this-timestamp language 3 · why (the check or the quote)Check 0:51 for a specific claim, spec or number viewers wanted to re-hear — replay peaks this early usually sit on a concrete detail dropped fast. 4 · how (the next move)Identify what is said at 0:51 and mirror that phrasing pattern earlier, inside the 0:15-0:26 stretch where the intro is bleeding. 5 · rationaleThe intro loses hard while this beat pulls people back, so the retention-earning content already exists — it just lands too late to save the open.
peak1:10

peak1:52
1 · what the curve showedThree viewers scrub back past the midpoint and the lift holds two samples, with 56.7% present (*55% vs similar videos*). 2 · evidence at that secondno transcript line available; the note uses check-this-timestamp language 3 · why (the check or the quote)Check 1:52 for a summary line, a comparison or a verdict — a peak that holds for two samples usually sits on a stated conclusion viewers wanted to confirm. 4 · how (the next move)Tease this line inside the first 30 seconds as an unresolved question, so new viewers stay to hear it delivered at 1:52. 5 · rationaleDopamine spikes at the announcement of a reward — front-loading the tease converts a mid-video asset into an intro-retention lever.

drop0:16
1 · what the curve showedThe first 18 seconds burn through the room faster than the channel's usual open (*13.60% stop rate vs 8.44% typical, 1.6x channel norm, 62 viewers gone*). 2 · evidence at that secondno transcript line available; the note uses check-this-timestamp language 3 · why (the check or the quote)Check 0:16-0:34 for a channel greeting, logo sting, or premise restatement that the thumbnail already sold. 4 · how (the next move)Cut 0:16-0:34 and open cold on the hardest failure moment from later in the build, then state the goal in one sentence. 5 · rationaleOpening on an out-of-context conflict beat is what the channel's best intro ("I built a MODERN XBOX...") does, and it protects the first-minute cap on AVD.
drop8:57
1 · what the curve showedA 17-second beat a third of the way in quits at nearly three times the channel's usual rate for this position (*9.7x local spike, 2.8x channel norm, 6 viewers lost*). 2 · evidence at that secondno transcript line available; the note uses check-this-timestamp language 3 · why (the check or the quote)Check 8:57-9:13 for a segue, tool swap, or verbal recap that pauses the build progression. 4 · how (the next move)Tighten 8:57-9:13 to under 5 seconds and land straight on the next physical action or decision. 5 · rationaleSomething should visibly change every ~5 seconds; the channel norm of 0.71% stop rate here proves viewers do not usually leave at this position.
drop12:51
1 · what the curve showedA 34-second stretch near the midpoint quits at more than six times the channel's usual rate here (*9.1x local spike, 6.3x channel norm, 15 viewers lost, audience 34.5% to 27.2%*). 2 · evidence at that secondno transcript line available; the note uses check-this-timestamp language 3 · why (the check or the quote)Check 12:51-13:25 for a static beat with no new information — likely a teardown, cable-management pass, or recap of a step already shown. 4 · how (the next move)Cut 12:51-13:25 down to a 5-second time-lapse and cross-cut the next build step over it so something visibly changes every few seconds. 5 · rationaleStripping-down phases lose people; pacing is the flow of NEW information, and the surrounding channel norm shows viewers do not normally quit here. cautionVerify the segment is not the setup a later reveal depends on; if it is, keep the payoff cue and trim only the dead middle.
peak19:17
1 · what the curve showedA single-sample bump 69% through the video adds 3 viewers (*+3.7% of audience present, held 1 sample, audience 34.1%*). 2 · evidence at that secondno transcript line available; the note uses check-this-timestamp language 3 · why (the check or the quote)Check 19:17 for a one-line reveal or measurement — the one-sample hold is a weak signal that may be a scrub target. 4 · how (the next move)Test extending this beat by 10 seconds with a riser starting 20 seconds before, and measure whether retention flattens through it. 5 · rationaleA single-sample tick is a data artifact until proven otherwise; anticipatory risers hold up to 10% more of the room into a payoff. cautionOne-sample peaks can be scrub-back to a specific frame rather than a loved moment; if the extended version does not flatten the curve, revert.
peak23:45
1 · what the curve showedThe audience rises and stays up for eight samples in a row (*+5.3% of audience present, 4 viewers regained, held 8 samples, audience 32.5%*). 2 · evidence at that secondno transcript line available; the note uses check-this-timestamp language 3 · why (the check or the quote)Check 23:45 for the payoff sequence viewers rewind to — likely the first successful power-on or a performance number. 4 · how (the next move)Move any outro plugs or thanks off this beat and hand straight to the next video within 20 seconds of the peak. 5 · rationaleRetention drops the moment viewers sense the video is ending, so the eight-sample hold here must not be spent on a wrap-up signal.
peak24:19
